prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which thousands of atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated at once, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B045 to B022. In round 1 I said I would sooner see the lattice clock awarded cleanly than force a contested three-name list, and the exchange has made that condition real. The topological credit is still unresolved after round 1: the committee has not agreed whether the unit is the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or topological insulators generally, Olsson wants Hasan in and Mele out, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D theory remain outside any trio. I cannot settle that from memory, and no one in the discussion has offered documentation that would. The lattice clock has no such problem. The magic-wavelength condition lets one interrogate thousands of atoms with no first-order light shift, which is a non-obvious physical result, not a refinement of an existing instrument. It has been reproduced by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) and checked by direct clock-to-clock comparison, which is the kind of independent confirmation I always ask for. It already produces physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and limits on varying constants and dark matter. Katori for the concept and first strontium demonstration and Ye for taking it to record accuracy is a two-name credit with no arbitrary cut. As a theorist I also note that the systematic shifts (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarisability) are computed from atomic structure theory and then confirmed by experiment, which is the quantitative theory-experiment link I value. Five of eight members already name this configuration with identical laureates. I am not following the count; I am moving because the scientific case is mature and the credit is clean.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems is real, and the citation must say that the new element is the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice, not combs, ion clocks or clocks in general. I am also concerned that a clock can be read as a better instrument rather than a discovery about nature. Danielsson and Mehlig are right that the constants and dark-matter searches have so far produced limits, not detections. Priority is not airtight: Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Ovsiannikov and others are outside the two names, and I defer to Lindroth and Olsson, who know this field, on whether the early strontium lattice papers fit the concept-and-performance split. The redefinition of the second has not happened. Finally, I give up what I still regard as a field-level change, band topology, in favour of the cleaner case, and I accept that this may be a loss for the physics.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first on the strength of independent laboratories agreeing at the 1e-18 level, and treats it as a distinct step beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes. In round 1 she and Olsson asked for expert checking of the early strontium lattice papers before the two names are settled.
responses.response: I am now persuaded by this case and have moved to it. Your emphasis on independent agreement is the criterion I weigh most, and it is met here more fully than for topological insulators, where the credit question is open. I would ask you, as the atomic physicist, to confirm for the committee that the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock are Katori's, and that Ye's group made the decisive accuracy step, and to say whether Lemonde's and Ludlow's work is a parallel route to the same result or a contribution that changes the names. If your answer is that it changes the names, I would want to know before the final ballot, since I cannot judge it myself.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B022 and ranks B045 as an alternative, but with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan instead of Mele. She argues that the Kane-Mele trio credits theory twice and leaves out the first 3D ARPES observation, and she asks for expert checking of priority among the lattice-clock groups.
responses.response: I still disagree with removing Mele, since Kane and Mele's two papers contain the Z2 classification that underlies both the 2D and 3D cases, so I do not think we agree on a B045 trio. But your Hasan point and the question of 2D versus 3D are exactly the unresolved attribution that moves me towards B022. I could accept your Hasan configuration only if the committee decides that the 3D discovery is the unit, and then Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy become hard to leave out. For B022 I share your request for documentary checking of the strontium priority, and I would support the citation wording you used, 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock', with the magic wavelength and the 10^-18 level named.

responses.point: Mehlig supports the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio but names B022 as his first alternative and calls it the safer prize if a clean, uncontested allocation is weighted above field-level influence. He also finds the distinction between the 2016 prize and B045 defensible but not self-evident.
responses.response: We have reached the same position from the same trio, and I think we should say so plainly. Your condition, that a clean allocation outweighs field-level influence when the credit cannot be documented, is the condition I accept. I still think the 2016 prize left room, because it covered defects, phase transitions and Haldane's chain, while this is symmetry-protected band topology in real materials, but I agree that the argument is not self-evident and would require a very careful citation. On the clock, I also take your point that magic-wavelength trapping builds on known atomic physics. My answer is that the many-atom, shift-free interrogation was not a known result, and the 10^-18 accuracy rests on that.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers baryon acoustic oscillations and says this first place reflects his own weighting, not a committee view. He asks whether a lattice clock tells us something unexpected about nature, since the constants and dark-matter results so far are limits, and he raises the question of a third cosmology prize after 2006, 2011 and 2019. He would not block B022.
responses.response: I take your criterion seriously, and I admit that for the clock the unexpected finding is the 10^-18 regime itself, not a detection of new physics. I think that is a physics result, since millimetre-scale redshift and clock comparisons across institutes are measurements of nature that no one could make before. That said, I accept that the committee should not call it a discovery of new physics. I do not think B002 should be ruled out because it is a third cosmology prize, and I defer to you on its science. My difficulty is that two survey collaborations made the detection and the theory predecessors (Peebles and Yu, Sunyaev and Zeldovich) are outside the trio, so credit is the same kind of problem I have just left in B045.

responses.point: Pearce, the Chair, now prefers B022 over his own opening first choice IceCube, and describes Katori for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for record accuracy as a clean two-person attribution. He drafts a citation for the lattice clock that brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level, and asks for precision on what is new compared with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the citation wording that names what is new, and I have written mine around the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice and not clocks in general. On the redefinition of the second, I agree that recognition does not need to wait, and that the physics has been established independently of any metrological decision. I would add that I do not think B046 should be ruled out by this discussion alone, but the questions Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson raise about two names for a collaboration of about 300 people are fair, and I would not support it before those roles are documented.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names, given Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and others. I am not an expert in atomic physics and I rely on Lindroth, Olsson and Kroll, and on documentary checking, for priority.
Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, which depends on the wording of one citation.

Whether I am giving up too much by moving away from topological insulators. My field bias may have made me overrate it, and my recollection of the Kane-Mele, BHZ, Konig and Hasan credit history is from memory and unchecked.
Whether the lattice clock should be called a discovery or an invention. I weight the independent reproduction and the tests of nature it enables, but I recognise that others weight it differently.
Whether magic-angle graphene (B030) will be mature enough in a few years, given the pairing-mechanism debate and twist-angle disorder.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has changed. I am a theorist in electronic-structure theory and magnetism, I have no known personal, institutional or collaborative tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist, and the lattice clock is outside my field. My earlier same-field interest in topological band theory (B045) is no longer relevant to my preferred configuration, but I continue to disclose it, and I defer to atomic-physics members on the B022 credit.
